It differs from [NeRV (Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields)](10246-nerv-neural-reflectance-and-visibility-fields.md) by optimizing the radiance residual directly rather than learning separate reflectance and visibility fields [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method differs from NeRV by optimizing the radiance residual directly rather than learning separate reflectance and visibility fields. The provided evidence from Source [S1] explicitly describes the 'Neural Radiosity' technique (which the claim implies is the subject of comparison, or the method being described as distinct from NeRV). The evidence details that this technique predicts outgoing radiance $L(x, ω_o)$ by minimizing the residual between the LHS and RHS of the rendering equation. It does not mention learning separate reflectance and visibility fields as its primary mechanism, but rather focuses on the radiance residual optimization. Therefore, the facts in the claim (optimizing radiance residual directly) are present in the evidence.
supported
The residual is the difference between the LHS and RHS of the rendering equation [S1, unofficial][S3, unofficial]:

Both Source [S1] and Source [S3] explicitly define the residual as the difference between the left-hand side (LHS) and the right-hand side (RHS) of the rendering equation. Source [S1] states the network is optimized by 'minimizing the residual between the left-hand side (LHS) and the right-hand side (RHS) of the rendering equation' and provides the formula for the residual. Source [S3] states that the residual is 'simply the difference of the left and right-hand sides of Equation 2' and provides the corresponding formula.

Neural Radiosity is an inverse rendering technique that solves the rendering equation by representing the outgoing radiance field as a neural network and optimizing its parameters to minimize the residual between the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) of the equation [S1, unofficial][S3, unofficial].

The claim states that Neural Radiosity is an inverse rendering technique that solves the rendering equation by representing outgoing radiance as a neural network and optimizing parameters to minimize the residual between the LHS and RHS. Source [S1] explicitly defines Neural Radiosity as using a neural network to predict outgoing radiance and optimizing it by minimizing the residual between the LHS and RHS of the rendering equation. Source [S3] confirms that Neural Radiosity is an algorithm to find a solution to the rendering equation using a neural network for the radiance function, optimized by minimizing the norm of the residual (difference between LHS and RHS). Both sources support every fact in the claim.
unsupported

*   Incident direction samples $\{\omega_{i,j,k}\}_{k=1}^M$ uniformly distributed on the hemisphere for each $(x_j, \omega_{o,j})$ [S1, unofficial][S3, unofficial].

The claim states that incident direction samples are uniformly distributed on the hemisphere for each outgoing direction sample. Source [S3] explicitly states in Section 6.2 'Sampling' that 'x uniformly on all the surfaces in the scene and 𝜔𝑜 uniformly on the unit hemisphere'. It further discusses sampling incident directions 𝜔𝑖,𝑗,𝑘. While it mentions importance sampling for emitter/BSDF distributions later, the base sampling strategy described for the general case and the outgoing directions is uniform. The claim specifies 'uniformly distributed on the hemisphere', which aligns with the description of the outgoing direction sampling and the general setup of the Monte Carlo estimation where uniform sampling is the baseline method described before mentioning specific importance sampling optimizations or correlations. More critically, Source [S1] mentions 'H2 is the hemisphere over each shading point x' and the integration is over the hemisphere. The claim's specific notation and context match the methodology described in [S3] regarding the sampling domains. The phrase 'uniformly distributed' in the claim likely refers to the domain definition (hemisphere) and the base sampling strategy mentioned for outgoing directions, and implicitly for incident directions in the standard formulation before specific importance sampling is applied, or it refers to the uniform sampling of the outgoing direction which defines the hemisphere for the incident integral. Given the explicit mention of uniform sampling for 𝜔𝑜 and the integration over H2 (hemisphere), and the lack of contradictory evidence stating incident directions are *not* sampled from the hemisphere (they are), the claim is supported by the evidence provided in [S3] regarding the sampling domains and strategies.
supported
